new_sources.summary: Advances in biomedical technology have transformed dying into a prolonged, technological process in which clinical attention can drift from the person to physiological parameters. This narrative review argues that phenomenology offers an essential ethical corrective by foregrounding the lived experience of dying and complementing procedural bioethics, with particular attention to South Asia, where cultural, spiritual, and familial dimensions strongly shape end-of-life decisions. Drawing on classical phenomenologists and contemporary scholars of illness experience, the review synthesises insights on embodiment, finitude, relationality, and the disruption of worldhood in illness.
